RagShortTexts: Heating birch bark yields tar and requires fuel, vessels and labour.
Tar dressing and seam repairs serve different needs; coating cannot mend torn leather.

Variants.Content:
Birch supplies more than bark notes and firewood: heating its bark can produce thick, strongly scented tar. Production needs controlled heat, a collecting vessel and a covering arrangement so that the product is not burnt away or contaminated with ash and earth. Damp bark, the fire and the vessel affect the yield; workers judge suitability through appearance, flow and smell.

Tar can dress leather and wooden articles, but coating is different from mending. A split sole still needs repair and a broken strap replacement. Excess tar stains clothes, collects dirt and gives cargo an odour. Buyers inspect impurities and closures; a leaking container can spoil nearby cloth as well as waste its contents.
Estates and caravans buying tar must also budget for vessels, transport and repair materials. Tar alone cannot restore harness without thread, leather and time.
Wet shoes, saddlery and reins need drying and inspection. Dressing a surface cannot repair a load-bearing break; finding a split before departure avoids a failure on the road.
Tar workers gather bark and fuel and tie up household vessels. Repairing a neighbour’s shoes involves separate leather, stitching and dressing work, beyond the amount of black liquid used.
